#Potential Analyses

#1.Statistics

I plan to calculate summary statistics for attendance, including the mean, median and standard deviation. I would calculate these separately for Maryland home games following a win and home games following a loss. I would also find the number of games in each group and comparing these statistics would give me an initial idea of whether attendance is higher following wins or losses. 

#2.Charts

I could create a bar chart comparing average attendance following wins and losses. This would provide a visual representation of the difference between the two groups.

I could also create a scatterplot comparing the number of days between games with attendance at the next home game. This would help me see whether there is a strong/weak/or no relationship between the two variables. I could use these charts to identify patterns before looking more closely at the statistics.

#3.Correlation

Correlation could be useful for examining the relationship between the number of days between games and attendance. Since both are numerical variables, I could calculate a correlation coefficient to determine whether there is a positive or negative relationship. This could help me investigate my second hypothesis.

I do not think correlation would be as useful for comparing wins and losses because the previous game result is categoricaland not numerical.


# Questions/ things I might need clarification on 

I need clarification on how to best compare attendance after wins and losses, especially if there are different numbers of games in each group. I am also unsure how to account for the number of days between games and whether comparing averages or calculating correlation would be the most useful approach for my second hypothesis.(Is the second hypothesis even worth including or should I stick to one and just scrap the other?)





#Research Question 

Does Maryland football attendance at regular-season home games vary depending on the outcome of the team's previous game?

#Hypothesis
#Hypothesis 1: 
Maryland home games following a win will have higher attendance on average than home games following a loss.
#Hypothesis 2: 
The relationship between Maryland's previous game result and attendance at its next home game will vary depending on the number of days between games.
#Data and Sources Links

My primary source is the cfbfastR-data GitHub repository, which contains annual CSV files with individual college football game records.(https://github.com/sportsdataverse/cfbfastR-data)

CSV files: https://github.com/sportsdataverse/cfbfastR-data/tree/main/schedules/csv

I plan to use the files from 2011 through 2025. They contain information such as game dates, teams, scores and attendance.

I will also use the CollegeFootballData API documentation to get data that is Maryland specific (when I can figure out how to use API because that is what the site uses to retrieve data, but we haven't gone over that and I couldn't figure it out, so I'm just putting it aside for now and will try to figure it out later):

# Filtering for UMD games only

```{r}
maryland_games <- games_all |>
  filter(home_team == "Maryland" | away_team == "Maryland")
```

```{r}
maryland_games |> count(season)
```

# UMD game data

```{r}
maryland_games <- maryland_games |>
mutate( maryland_points = ifelse(home_team == "Maryland", home_points, away_points),
opponent_points = ifelse(home_team == "Maryland", away_points, home_points),
maryland_home = home_team == "Maryland",
maryland_win = maryland_points > opponent_points
  )
```

# Previous game results 
```{r}
maryland_games <- maryland_games |>
  filter(season_type == "regular") |>
  arrange(season, start_date) |>
  group_by(season) |>mutate(
  previous_result = lag(maryland_win),
  days_between_games = as.numeric(start_date - lag(start_date))
  )
```
```{r}
attendance_analysis <- maryland_games |>
  filter(maryland_home == TRUE,
  !is.na(previous_result),
  !is.na(attendance),
  attendance > 0
  )
```

```{r}
attendance_analysis |>
  count(previous_result)
```

# I used `count()` to determine how many Maryland home games followed a win and how many followed a loss. This helped me see how many games were included in each group before comparing their attendance.

# average attendance statistics
```{r}
attendance_analysis |>
  group_by(previous_result) |>
  summarise(
    mean_attendance = mean(attendance),
    sd_attendance = sd(attendance)
  )
```
#I used `summarise()` to calculate the mean attendance and standard deviation for each group. The average attendance was slightly higher following a Maryland loss than following a win, which was the opposite of what I originally expected,but the difference between the two averages was relatively small. 

# Attendance after wins and losses 

```{r}
attendance_analysis |>
  group_by(previous_result) |>
  summarise(mean_attendance = mean(attendance)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = previous_result, y = mean_attendance)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("FALSE" = "Loss", "TRUE" = "Win")) +
  labs(title = "Average Maryland Football Attendance After Wins and Losses",
    x = "Previous Game Result",
    y = "Average Attendance"
  )
```
# The bar graph makes the difference in average attendance easier to compare. It shows that attendance was slightly higher after a loss than after a win. Again, this does not support my original hypothesis that attendance would be higher following a win.

# Attendance and time between gamms scatterplot 
```{r}
ggplot(attendance_analysis, aes(x = days_between_games, y = attendance)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Maryland Football Attendance and Time Between Games",
    x = "Days Between Games",
    y = "Home Game Attendance"
  )
```
# I also created a scatterplot to examine whether the number of days between Maryland games was related to attendance. Most of the games were approximately a week apart. The graph does not show an obvious relationship between the time between games and attendance.
